clue.text: Record vehicle at home, one constructed of wood

blocks.note: a log is a written record, as in a ship's log
a cab is a taxi, a vehicle
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Someone logs a vehicle parked at home, then mentions something made of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end as a descriptive phrase; the three short pieces run straight on in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional frontier hut is built from whole tree trunks laid horizontally, so it is literally made of timber.

clue.text: Dominate circle with part of speech, getting attention

blocks.note: a circle is shaped like the letter O
a verb is one of the grammatical parts of speech
to have someone's ear is to have their attention

explanation.surface: Someone dominates a group by making a speech and getting everyone's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of speech' looks like a slice of an oration, but it is the grammar term: a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To overbear is to overwhelm or bully others by sheer weight of personality, a close synonym.

clue.text: Odd concern — a duty that’s performed in sets

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the noun: a thing performed in sets

indicators.note: something odd is strange or out of order, so the following words are jumbled

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, the dash ignored

explanation.surface: A strange business: some duty that has to be carried out in batches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sets' reads like batches of work, but dancers form up in sets: groups of couples facing each other for a reel or jig.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional folk dances are danced by groups of couples arranged in lines or squares, each group called a set.

clue.text: Badly behaved without reason around ring-leader

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: batty means crazy, lacking reason
the first letter of ring

explanation.surface: A gang's ring-leader behaves badly for no reason at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring-leader' is a single word in the surface, the head of a gang, but here it means the first letter of 'ring'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoilt, unruly child is a brat, and the adjective describes that kind of naughty conduct.

clue.text: One’s perturbed about king that’s a tyrannical ruler

indicators.note: a perturbed thing is disturbed and upset, so the letters of 'One' get rearranged
the rearranged word goes about, surrounding, the royal letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A worried courtier frets about a monarch who rules like a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'One' is just 'is', part of the surface grammar; the three letters of 'One' split around the king.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman emperor of the first century is remembered as a cruel despot who, legend says, fiddled while Rome burned.

clue.text: Figure of speech, oddly, to hamper or harm poet

indicators.note: done oddly means done in a strange, disordered way, so the words that follow are jumbled

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A figure of speech might be used, strangely, to hinder or wound a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: A double bluff: 'to hamper' and 'harm poet' are each an exact anagram of METAPHOR, so the setter offers two alternative fodders joined by 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing one thing as though it were another, like calling life a journey, is a classic rhetorical device.

clue.text: Bad upset, as it happens

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset something is to turn it upside down, so the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: evil means bad

explanation.surface: Someone is badly upset, just as the event unfolds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad upset' reads as one phrase about distress; split it, and 'upset' flips the word for wicked.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast shown in real time, not recorded, is transmitted at the very moment of the event.

clue.text: People agree that’s how to do brain operations

blocks.note: men are people
figures that tally agree with each other

explanation.surface: People agree on the right way to perform brain surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brain operations' suggests surgery, but it means thinking: sums done in the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Working something out in the head, without paper, is doing it with the mind; the adverb names that manner.

clue.text: Work out duty guarding monarch

indicators.note: to guard something is to surround and protect it

blocks.note: excise is a duty, a tax on goods
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone works out their duty while guarding the monarch, like a palace sentry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work out' could mean solve, but here it is a verb for training the body; the tax word splits after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To exercise is to train physically at the gym, exactly what working out means in everyday speech.

clue.text: Finishing up the tour, you land in South America

indicators.note: the finishing letter of a word is its last one, so take the end of each of the next four words

blocks.note: the last letters of up, the, tour and you

explanation.surface: A traveller finishes a tour and lands in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finishing up' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'up' is the first of the four words whose final letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andean republic on the Pacific coast, home of Machu Picchu, is a country on that continent.

clue.text: Mingled to blend in, at a thing that’s outstanding for all of us

definitions.text: thing that’s outstanding for all of us

indicators.note: things mingled are mixed together, so the letters that follow are stirred

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, the comma ignored

explanation.surface: Someone mingles to fit in at a party, then admires something brilliant for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' seems to mean excellent; here it means unpaid, still owed.
explanation.definitionFit: The money a government owes on behalf of every citizen remains unpaid, a shared liability of the whole country.

clue.text: Completed taking in broken nets, with fish extricated

blocks.note: did means carried out, completed
anagram fodder
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: Fishermen finish hauling in torn nets and free the trapped fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two inserted pieces; both go inside the word for completed.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeing something from a knot or tangle is exactly what extricating means: releasing it from a snare.

clue.text: Agreement to contain fight in settlement

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within

blocks.note: a deal is an agreement
a fray is a brawl or fight

explanation.surface: A peace agreement is meant to contain fighting in a disputed settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settlement' reads as a village; here it is the paying of a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: To defray costs is to pay them, so the noun is the payment or discharging of a bill or account.

clue.text: Allowed supporter to go over a line

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece going over another sits above it, so the limb comes first

blocks.note: a leg supports a table or a body
as printed
L is a standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A fan is permitted to cross a line, perhaps onto the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' looks like a football fan; it is the thing that holds you up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something permitted by law is lawful, so the adjective for lawful is a direct synonym of permitted.

clue.text: Son’s in one kind of accommodation or another

definitions.note: short for 'another kind of accommodation', a noun

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
a hotel is one kind of lodging

explanation.surface: A son is staying in some kind of lodging or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One kind of accommodation' is the wordplay, a hotel; the definition is the final 'another', meaning a second kind of lodging made by putting the son inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A budget lodging house with shared dormitories for young travellers is a different type of place to stay from a hotel.

clue.text: Stimulate or pressure staff

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
a staff is a stick or rod

explanation.surface: A manager must choose whether to motivate or lean on employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees; here it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: To poke someone into action is to urge or goad them, a figurative sense of spurring on.

clue.text: Step over weapon that’s required by sentry

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the noun: the thing a sentry requires

blocks.note: a pas is a step in ballet
a sword is a weapon

explanation.surface: A soldier steps over a weapon that a sentry needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step' is the French ballet word pas, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A guard on duty demands a secret word before letting anyone pass, so it is what the sentry insists on hearing.

clue.text: Full of enthusiasm, agree to differ

indicators.note: letters made to differ from their order become a different arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Two keen people cheerfully agree to differ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agree to differ' is a set phrase, but 'to differ' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen and impatient to do something is the adjective's sense, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Never stopping to collect vote outside

blocks.note: eternal means endless, never stopping
a cross, X, marks a vote on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A tireless canvasser keeps going to gather votes outside.
explanation.walkthrough: X for vote comes from the cross made on a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the outer side or surface of a thing is exterior, the adjective's plain meaning.

clue.text: Boy reversing his conclusion — that’s curious

indicators.note: reversing means running backwards

blocks.note: a son is a boy
'his' is the boy, and the conclusion of that word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A boy changes his mind, and the reversal is odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His conclusion' is the boy's end, the final letter of 'Boy', not of the word 'his'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inquisitive about other people's business, prying, is the informal sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Was a tourist making sense with proverb?

blocks.note: sight is one of the five senses
a saw is an old saying, a proverb

explanation.surface: A tourist tries to make sense of a local proverb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the two pieces; 'saw' as a proverb is an old sense worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Visiting famous places as a sightseer is what holidaymakers do, and the verb's past tense fits the clue.

clue.text: Instrument made of wood set in stone

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, a British unit of weight
pine is a kind of wood

explanation.surface: An instrument crafted from wood is mounted in a stone setting.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds, abbreviated st; 'made of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small harpsichord with a single keyboard is a keyboard musical instrument popular in earlier centuries.

clue.text: Greatly agitated about hospital’s inertia

indicators.note: something agitated is shaken up
the shaken word goes about

blocks.note: anagram fodder
H is the abbreviation for hospital on maps and road signs

explanation.surface: Someone is very worked up about a hospital's sluggishness.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of hospital's is only surface grammar; 'Greatly' is fodder, not an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of sluggishness and lack of energy is torpor, the listless inactivity that inertia describes.

clue.text: Awful oil ingested by rat turning up in sewer

indicators.note: awful means dreadful, a bad state
in a down clue, turning up makes the word read from bottom to top
what is ingested is swallowed inside

blocks.note: anagram fodder
as printed

explanation.surface: A sewer rat swallows some nasty oil it finds in the drains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' is a drain in the surface but here means one who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who stitches and makes clothes for a living is one who sews, so the garment maker is a sewer.

clue.text: Is accepted into partnership with excellent badinage

indicators.note: something accepted into a group is taken inside it

blocks.note: as printed
in bridge, West and East play as partners
cracking is British slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A newcomer joins a firm whose members trade superb banter.
explanation.walkthrough: In the card game bridge the four players are North, South, East and West, and East-West form one partnership.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading quick jokes and witty remarks is playful banter, which is what badinage names.

clue.text: Set of clothes in case

blocks.note: a matching jacket and trousers or skirt
a lawsuit is a case brought in court

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is legal: a suit is a lawsuit, a case in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching jacket and trousers form one outfit, while a lawsuit is a court action brought against someone.

clue.text: Damage bed in nursery inserting spades

indicators.note: inserting puts something inside

blocks.note: a cot is a baby's bed
S abbreviates spades, the card suit

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks a nursery bed by digging into it with spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damage' is the informal noun for price, as in 'what's the damage?'; spades are the card suit, not tools.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking the price of a bill jokingly as its harm to your wallet is a colloquial sense meaning the amount charged.

clue.text: Miss lesson in school when head’s away

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, and with it away the word loses its opening

blocks.note: a class is a school lesson; drop its first letter

explanation.surface: A pupil skips a lesson while the headteacher is out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb, to skip class, but it is a noun for a young woman; 'head' is the first letter, not the headteacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A young unmarried woman is addressed as Miss, and the Scottish or northern word for a girl means the same.

clue.text: Transport systems run without fail around one

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
always means every time, without fail
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Transport networks run reliably all around one region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' reads as operate; it is the cricket scoring abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Networks of tracks on which trains carry passengers and freight are systems for moving people and goods.

clue.text: Reject move — what’s next?

blocks.note: in a game, your turn is your move
this is the last across clue, so the down clues come next

explanation.surface: A player refuses a move and asks what comes next.
explanation.walkthrough: A self-referential joke: after the final across clue a solver moves on to the downs.
explanation.definitionFit: To decline an offer or invitation is to refuse it, the phrasal verb's common meaning.
